newsitem.title: HONG KONG: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - China Int'l Marine nets FRN.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - China Int'l Marine nets FRN.

text.p: China International Marine launched a US$40 million floating rate note into Asian primary debt markets on Wednesday, while in the secondary markets reaction to bad news from South Korea was muted.
The US$40 million notes for China International Marine mature in five years but can be put on the third anniversary.
They were launched at par to float at 100 basis points over the six-month London Interbank Offered Rate.
Societe Generale Asia is the lead.
With fees, the all-in return to top-tier managers is 111.6 basis points.
The Shenzhen-listed company is major manufacturere of ship containers. It is 23 percent owned by COSCO and 23 percent owned by China Merchants Holdings.
Florens Container Corp, a container-maker wholly owned by Cosco Pacific, has a US$200 million loan in syndication that is expected to be completed next week.
News of new issues was otherwise sparse, though a few new deals should be launched into London markets soon.
The one-year 3.0 billion Philippine peso Eurobond of the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) may launch as early as today via lead manager ING Barings.
The World Bank and International Finance Corp separately issued the first peso Eurobonds last week to wide acclaim. Both of those issues had five-year tenors.
Traders said Korean credits traded in the secondary market showed little reaction to the latest news from South Korea, not because the news wasn't bad but because the debt just isn't trading.
South Korea's Sammi Steel Co sought protection from its creditors along with four other affiliates of Sammi Group, South Korea's 26th largest conglomerate.
The move was another blow to the country's banking sector, which was hit hard by the collapse of Hanbo Steel in January.
"We could see more selling in London," said one trader, who predicted that Korean banks' debt traded in the secondary market will continue its weakening trend.

Those Korean banks that have braved the international capital markets in the wake of the Hanbo crisis have seen their borrowing costs rise significantly. And outstanding debt of Korean banks has been trading poorly.
Outstanding floating rate notes of Korea First Bank, which is the largest creditor to both Sammi and Hanbo, have suffered greatly in the secondary markets.
For example, Korea First paper with a remaining life of about three years was trading in the high 70s over LIBOR, whereas three-year notes launched late last year were priced in the mid-40s.

Bankers said Korean banks could find their funding costs rising further. In addition, some expressed fears that Korean banks, which have become aggressive investors in other Asian debt, may start withdrawing from the market.
In other news, Siam City Bank has delayed its issue of US$100 million in FRCDs pending Moody's Investors Services assessment of Thailand's sovereign rating.
